title: Acute compartment syndrome of the limb
subject: surgery-trauma
setting: Emergency department, orthopaedic ward, theatre recovery, ICU
summary: Suspect it with pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch; release every circumferential dressing and cast down to skin, measure compartment pressure when examination is unreliable (delta pressure below 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis), and perform immediate fasciotomy of all involved compartments once diagnosed (BOAST 2025).

sections.title: Recognise
items: It is a clinical diagnosis; pressure measurement supports it when examination is inconclusive or not possible.
Key early findings: pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment, and a rising analgesic requirement.
Later findings: paraesthesia, tense swollen compartment, weakness. Pallor and absent pulses are late; palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.

High-risk settings: tibial shaft and forearm fractures, crush injury, high-energy trauma, reperfusion after vascular repair, tight casts or dressings, prolonged limb compression (found collapsed), burns, and infusion extravasation.
Examination is unreliable in patients who are unconscious, sedated, intoxicated, or under regional anaesthesia; they need pressure monitoring.
Viper bite: massive swelling is common but true compartment syndrome is rare. Give antivenom and correct coagulopathy; consider fasciotomy only if raised compartment pressure is proven.

sections.title: Immediate actions
items: Release all circumferential dressings, casts and padding right down to the skin (split the cast and padding completely).
Elevate the limb and re-evaluate within 30 minutes (BOAST 2025).
Correct hypotension and hypoxia, because a low blood pressure reduces tissue perfusion pressure.
Get immediate review by a senior surgeon with decision-making authority, and record the dose and timing of all analgesics, particularly opioids.
Keep the patient nil by mouth while the decision about fasciotomy is made.

sections.title: Compartment pressure measurement
items: Measure intracompartmental pressure in all suspected compartments when clinical signs are inconclusive or assessment is not possible, with blood pressure recorded at the same time.

Delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) below 30 mmHg indicates increased risk and, with the clinical picture, supports the diagnosis and the need for fasciotomy; it is not an absolute indication on its own. A compartment pressure above 40 mmHg should prompt consideration of urgent decompression. The decision rests with a consultant orthopaedic surgeon (BOAST 2025).
For tibial fractures where symptoms cannot be assessed (unconscious, nerve block), consider continuous compartment pressure monitoring (NICE NG37).
Send CK, creatinine, potassium and urinalysis for myoglobin; ECG if potassium is raised.

sections.title: Fasciotomy
items: Once the diagnosis is made, perform immediate surgical decompression (NCEPOD category 1); do not wait for imaging or for the pulse to disappear.
Open all involved compartments fully and debride non-viable muscle; document the appearance and viability of each compartment. Lower leg: two-incision, four-compartment fasciotomy.
Leave fasciotomy wounds open; discuss with plastic surgery within 24 hours and plan re-exploration within 72 hours, or earlier if needed.

Late presentation or diagnosis (established muscle necrosis): surgery carries high complication risk. Decide with two consultants; non-operative management with renal assessment and protection is an option.
Treat rhabdomyolysis with IV crystalloid to maintain a good urine output, and monitor potassium, creatinine and CK.

sections.title: Monitoring at-risk patients
items: Assess hourly and document findings (present or absent), their interpretation and the plan: time, level of consciousness, pain score, response to analgesia, and neurovascular status.
For tibial fractures, stay alert for compartment syndrome for 48 hours after injury or fixation, and teach patients to self-monitor after discharge (NICE NG37).
Regional anaesthesia after limb trauma needs a joint decision by the patient, anaesthetist and surgeon, and a clear plan for postoperative compartment monitoring.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Waiting for pallor, paralysis or pulselessness.
Escalating opioids for pain that is out of proportion instead of examining the limb.
Splitting the cast but not the padding underneath.
Relying on a single normal pressure reading when the clinical picture is worsening.
Foot compartment syndrome has no consensus management: document the reasoning for the plan chosen.

algorithms.title: Acute Compartment Syndrome Assessment and Decompression Pathway

steps.action: Patient with fracture, crush injury, tight cast, or reperfusion presenting with severe pain out of proportion to injury.
Immediately bivalve and completely remove all circumferential casts, splints, and compressive dressings down to bare skin. Maintain limb at heart level (do not elevate).
Measure compartment pressure with needle manometry. Calculate delta pressure = Diastolic BP minus measured Compartment Pressure.
Confirms Acute Compartment Syndrome. Inadequate tissue perfusion and evolving myonecrosis.
Emergent multi-compartment fasciotomy. For lower leg: 2-incision 4-compartment release (anterolateral and posteromedial). Delaying surgery > 6 hours causes irreversible neuromuscular disability.

algorithms.caption: Algorithm aligned with BOAST 2025 and British Orthopaedic Association guidance.

tables.title: Clinical Signs Sensitivity, Timing, and Diagnostic Value
rows: Earliest symptom; unresponsive to escalating opioid analgesia
Tension on ischaemic muscle fibres; crucial early sign in alert patients
Direct physical sign of elevated intracompartmental hydrostatic pressure
Sensory deficit in distribution of traversing nerves (e.g. webspace 1)
Indicates advanced motor nerve and muscle ischaemia; heralds irreversible tissue damage
Very low sensitivity (absent in most cases)
Terminal sign of complete arterial occlusion; never wait for pulselessness to diagnose
tables.caption: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; irreversible muscle necrosis occurs within 6 to 8 hours.
